teaser: Gauguin meant it as his last word before dying. Paris looked at it and asked what it meant.
review_notes:
The source image is small and very panoramic (960 px wide), so spots point at whole figures and groups, not fine details; the lizard under the bird's foot and the lettering of the inscription cannot be made out at this size.
First showing at Vollard's gallery, Paris, November-December 1898; André Fontainas's review in the Mercure de France (January 1899) and Gauguin's reply by letter (March 1899): the lesson paraphrases both, no direct quotes from Fontainas.
Vollard bought the group of paintings sent from Tahiti for 1,000 francs: verify.
Suicide attempt with arsenic in the mountains is known only from Gauguin's own letters to Daniel de Monfreid; presented as his account.
'Painted in a month, day and night, with no preparation' is Gauguin's claim; a squared preparatory drawing exists (Musée du quai Branly / former Musée des Arts d'Afrique et d'Océanie).
Meanings of figures (bird = futility of words, idol = the Beyond, old woman near death) come from Gauguin's letters.
Peruvian mummy (Trocadéro ethnographic museum) as source of the old woman's pose: widely accepted.
Three questions linked to Bishop Dupanloup's catechism at the Petit Séminaire near Orléans: common scholarly suggestion, verify wording.
Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, purchase 1936.
Dimensions about 139 x 375 cm.
Painting is dated 1897 on the canvas; work likely continued into early 1898.

lesson.text: In November 1898 a roll of coarse cloth from Tahiti was stretched and hung in Ambroise Vollard's small gallery in Paris. Visitors found a wall of deep blue and green nearly four meters long, crowded with figures who did not seem to be doing anything together. Some were moved by the color. Many were simply lost. What was the story?

The poet and critic André Fontainas put the complaint in print. He admired the harmony of the colors, but he wrote that nothing in the picture itself would explain the allegory if Paul Gauguin had not written a title in the corner. An allegory is a scene where figures stand for ideas. For Fontainas, this one did not speak clearly enough.

Gauguin read the review months later, on the other side of the world, and answered with a long letter. His painting was not meant to be decoded like a puzzle, he said. It should work like music, through color and line, before any explanation. The title was not a caption. It was a signature at the end of a dream.
Vollard bought this painting together with eight others from the same shipment for 1,000 francs in total. Gauguin, who learned of the deal by mail, was bitter about the price for years.

To see why he cared so much, go back one year. In 1897 Gauguin was forty-nine, living in a hut outside Papeete, sick, in debt and in pain from an old leg injury. In the spring a letter told him that his favorite child, Aline, had died of pneumonia in Copenhagen at nineteen. He stopped writing to his wife. By December he had decided to kill himself.

First, he wanted to leave a testament: one large painting that would hold everything he thought about life. He later told a friend that he worked on it day and night for a month, in a kind of fever, with no model and no preparation. Then, by his own account, he walked into the mountains and swallowed arsenic. He took too much, vomited it up, and survived.

He could not afford proper canvas. The picture is painted on rough sackcloth, the kind used for sacks, full of knots and wrinkles. Gauguin said the surface made the painting look terribly coarse, and he liked it that way.

The size is about 1.4 by 3.75 meters (4.5 by 12 feet), so you cannot take it in at once. Your eye has to travel. European pictures are usually read like a page, from left to right. Gauguin told his friends to read this one the other way.
Two directions organize the whole frieze.

lines.label: Right to left
lines.text: The story runs backward, from the baby at the lower right to the old woman at the far left. It is the direction of a human life, birth to death.

lines.label: The standing figure
lines.text: One upright body spans the full height of the picture and splits it in two. Everything else sits or crouches. This figure is the hinge of the composition.

lines.label: Two zones
lines.text: Below this line the figures glow orange and yellow on dark ground. Above it, everything turns blue and green: trees, sea, a far island. Warm life in front, cool mystery behind.

lesson.text: Each third of the picture answers one of the three questions in the title. On the right, where do we come from: a beginning. In the middle, what are we: daily life, with its appetite and its doubts. On the left, where are we going: old age and whatever follows. Gauguin described the stations himself in his letters.

lesson.title: A life, read backward
lesson.text: Four stops, from the right edge to the left.

spots.title: The sleeping child
spots.text: A baby lies on the ground at the lower right, watched over by three seated women. This is the start of the story, and the only figure completely at peace.

spots.title: Picking the fruit
spots.text: A young person reaches up to pick a fruit from a branch. It can recall Eve in the garden, but there is no shame here, only the plain act of living.

spots.title: Two in purple
spots.text: In the shadows behind, two robed figures walk and talk. Gauguin said they confide their thoughts to each other. They are the ones who ask the questions the others do not.

spots.title: The old woman
spots.text: At the far left an old woman sits curled up, hands to her face, skin gone gray-brown. Gauguin wrote that she is close to death and seems to accept it.

lesson.text: The crouching old woman did not come from Tahiti. Her pose is borrowed from a Peruvian mummy that Gauguin had seen in a Paris museum years before, and he reused it in several works. He carried a trunk of photographs and prints with him to the Pacific: Egyptian reliefs, Javanese temples, European paintings. This “Tahiti” is stitched together from all of them.
The painting is not a view of Tahiti. It is an invented frieze about the ages of life, meant to be felt through color before it is explained.

Even so, Gauguin planted a few figures that he did explain, and one of them is his reply, in advance, to anyone who would ask for a clear meaning. It stands in the last corner of the story, beside the old woman.
Gauguin said a strange white bird stands for “the futility of words.” Where is it?

spots.title: The white bird
spots.text: In the lower left corner, at the old woman's feet, a white bird holds a lizard under its claw. It is the last creature in the story, and it has nothing to say. That is its message.

lesson.text: A bird that means words are useless: no wonder the critics were stuck. Gauguin wanted it both ways. He gave hints, then insisted that hints were beside the point. What he trusted was the slow blue of the background and the gold of the bodies against it. The rest of the picture is yours to wander.

spots.title: The idol
spots.text: A pale blue statue raises both arms. It is no single Polynesian god. Gauguin said it points, with its mysterious rhythm, toward the Beyond.

spots.title: Listening
spots.text: A woman in a long dark dress stands beside the idol, turned away from it. Gauguin wrote that she seems to listen to it.

spots.title: The child
spots.text: A child sits on the ground eating a fruit, perhaps the one just picked overhead. Next to the child, two small white cats play.

spots.title: The huge back
spots.text: A seated figure seen from behind lifts an arm to its head. It is far larger than its neighbors. Gauguin broke the rules of perspective on purpose and said so.

spots.title: The young woman
spots.text: Leaning on one arm, she sits between the idol and the old woman. Youth and old age, placed side by side, with only a few inches of canvas between them.

spots.title: The black dog
spots.text: A dark dog lies at the right edge, facing into the scene. A dog like this turns up in many of Gauguin's Tahitian pictures, a silent onlooker that some read as the painter himself.

spots.title: The title
spots.text: The three questions are written in French in the yellow upper left corner. Gauguin wanted the corners to look like patches of an old gold wall showing through a damaged fresco.

spots.title: The other corner
spots.text: The matching yellow corner on the right carries the signature and the date, 1897.

lesson.text: The three questions may go back to Gauguin's school days. As a boy he boarded at a Catholic seminary near Orléans, where the bishop taught a catechism built on almost the same words: where does humanity come from, where is it going, how does it proceed?

Gauguin lived five more years and painted many more pictures, but he said he would never do anything better than this one, or even anything like it. He died in 1903 on the Marquesas Islands. The canvas passed through several collectors before the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston bought it in 1936.

Fontainas wanted a painting that explained itself. Gauguin offered three questions and a silent bird. More than a century later, visitors in Boston still walk the length of the canvas from right to left and reach the end without an answer. Perhaps that was the honest way to paint it.

quiz.question: What did the critic André Fontainas object to?
options: The meaning was unclear without the written title
quiz.explanation: He admired the color but felt the allegory could not be understood from the picture alone.

quiz.question: In which direction did Gauguin want the painting read?
quiz.explanation: The story runs from the baby at the right to the old woman at the left.

quiz.question: What is the picture painted on?
quiz.explanation: Gauguin could not afford canvas and used coarse sacking full of knots.

quiz.question: What does the white bird stand for, according to Gauguin?
quiz.explanation: He wrote that the strange bird represents the uselessness of words.

quiz.question: Where did the pose of the old woman come from?
options: A Peruvian mummy Gauguin saw in Paris
quiz.explanation: He borrowed the curled-up pose from a mummy in a Paris museum and reused it several times.

quiz.question: What news reached Gauguin in the spring of 1897?
quiz.explanation: Aline died of pneumonia at nineteen, and the loss pushed him toward despair.

facts.text: Gauguin intended this painting as a testament before taking his own life.
facts.explanation: By his own account he painted it in a month and then tried to poison himself with arsenic.

facts.text: The blue idol is an exact copy of a statue Gauguin found in a Tahitian temple.
facts.explanation: It is no single Polynesian god; Gauguin invented it to suggest the Beyond.

facts.text: The yellow corners were meant to look like a gold wall showing through a damaged fresco.
facts.explanation: Gauguin described the corners this way, and they hold the title and the signature.
